SFlash

v2.0 — User Guide
ECU firmware flashing over CAN using UDS (ISO 14229)

SFlash is a tool for flashing firmware onto an ECU over the CAN bus. You can try it with the Virtual ECU Simulator (no hardware required at all) to get familiar with the interface, or use real Vector VN1640A / VN1630 hardware to flash a real ECU.

This page only covers the basic flashing workflow through the GUI. For full technical details (real Vector hardware setup, the command-line interface, and more), see the accompanying README.md.

Single Flash Tab

The Single Flash tab has two modes, switched via Tools → Mode: Flash (one firmware file, one ECU) and Batch Flash (the same firmware flashed onto several ECUs, one after another, without leaving the tab).

Flash Mode

1

Load a firmware file

Go to Configure → Data (or use the menu File → Load Firmware...), click the "Please click here to add a Datablock" row, and pick a firmware file (.hex, .s19/.s3, or .bin). Once loaded, the file appears in the table with its checksum computed automatically — the checkbox at the start of each row toggles whether that file is included in the next flash run. Loaded a file before? Menu File → Recent Files lists the last few and reloads one with a single click, no need to browse again.

2

Configure the connection

Go to Configure → Communication: pick the Hardware (defaults to "Virtual ECU Simulator" — no hardware needed; or select a real Vector channel if hardware is already connected, using "Refresh" if it was plugged in after the app started), the Radar Side (S0/S1, matching the actual ECU being flashed), and the Logical Link (CAN/CAN FD). The table below shows the CAN ID/baudrate details, which can be edited by hand if needed.

3

Click Flash

Switch back to the Single Flash tab and click the Flash button in the top-left corner to start. The button turns into Abort while running — click it again to cancel partway through. If no firmware file has been loaded yet (step 1), the app will warn you and won't start.

4

Monitor progress & export a report

The table on the left shows each UDS step performed (turning green once done), while the table on the right tracks progress per segment. The Information/Trace tabs below show detailed logs. After the flash finishes (or at any time), use the menu Tools → Export Report → Single Flash... to save an HTML report summarizing the whole session — useful as evidence that the flash was done correctly.

Tip: the Tools → Test Connection... menu lets you safely verify session + security access (without touching Erase/Download) before trusting a real flash to it — very useful for confirming wiring/CAN IDs/the security algorithm on a real ECU for the first time.
Tip: prefer a darker interface? Toggle View → Dark Mode — the app remembers your choice for next time. The menu Edit also has Clear Information Log/Clear Trace Table to start a fresh log without restarting the app.

Batch Flash Mode

1

Switch to Batch Flash mode

Menu Tools → Mode → Batch Flash. A Batch Flash panel appears below the flash controls, with a running tally and a log table — one row per ECU. The main button changes from Flash to Start. Load the firmware and set the connection first, exactly as in steps 1–2 of Flash Mode: every ECU in the batch uses those same settings.

2

Connect the first ECU and click Start

Each ECU runs two stages back to back, with no click in between: Identify reads its Serial Number, then Flash writes the firmware. The step and segment tables fill in exactly as in single-flash mode, and the button reads Abort while the unit is running — aborting stops that ECU only, not the batch.

3

Swap in the next ECU and click Next

When a unit finishes, its result is appended to the log (PASS green, FAIL red, ABORTED amber) with its serial number and duration, the tally updates, and the button relabels to Next. Disconnect that ECU, connect the following one, and click Next. Repeat for as many units as you have.

4

Stop the batch and export the report

Stop Batch ends the session at any time. Export Report saves one HTML report covering every ECU in the session — each unit's serial number, result and duration, plus the totals — which is the record to keep for a production run. It is separate from Tools → Export Report, which only covers the most recent single flash.

Parallel Flash Tab

Flashes up to 6 ECUs at once — one per physical CAN channel, laid out as 6 cards (3 rows × 2 columns). Every channel runs on its own; none has to wait for another. The firmware and the CAN protocol settings are shared, taken from Configure just as in the other modes.

1

Assign a hardware channel to each card

Each card drives one ECU. Pick its hardware channel from the dropdown — the same list as Configure → Communication, including the Virtual ECU Simulator. Cards left on Not Selected stay out of the way: their buttons are disabled and they are skipped by everything below. Need different CAN IDs on one channel? Set them per card under … → Settings.

2

Check each channel with Test Connection

Test Connection probes just that channel — session and data reads only, never an erase or download — so it is safe to run before trusting a real ECU to it. The button turns green on a pass and red on a failure, and the color stays put, so you can see at a glance which channels are wired correctly before flashing anything.

3

Flash the channels

Flash on a card runs Identify then Flash for that channel alone; Start All at the top launches every ready channel at once. They run genuinely in parallel, each with its own progress bar and status line, so the channels sit at different points at the same moment. The dot in each header gives the state at a glance: gray idle, blue busy, green pass, red fail. Abort stops one channel; Abort All stops every running one.

4

Read the logs and export reports

Each card's … menu holds three per-channel actions: Settings (CAN IDs for that channel), View Log (show that channel's own Information and Trace history in the shared tabs below — the last line tells you which channel you are viewing), and Save Report (an HTML report for that one channel). For the whole board at once, use Tools → Export Report → Parallel Flash: one combined report covering every channel that has a hardware selection, skipping the ones left on Not Selected.

Loading Firmware from GitLab

As an alternative to picking a local file (step 1 above), SFlash can fetch the firmware directly from a GitLab CI job artifact or the GitLab Package Registry. Open it via File → Load from GitLab..., or the Load from GitLab button on Configure → Data.

Connection

Fill in the Instance URL and a personal Access Token with the read_api, read_registry, and (if required by project policy) read_repository scopes — the dialog shows this same hint. Both are shared by the two tabs below and remembered for next time. Only uncheck Verify TLS certificate for a self-hosted instance using a self-signed certificate — leave it checked otherwise. An optional Download folder (with Browse...) keeps the fetched firmware file permanently instead of the default temp folder that gets deleted once the dialog closes — set one so File → Recent Files can reopen the same file later.

CI Artifact tab

Enter the Project (e.g. group/ci-project) and, optionally, a Branch / tag — click Load branches/tags to pick from the repository's real list instead of typing one by hand. Then either Fetch Latest Artifact (grabs the newest matching job's artifact for the chosen branch/tag and job name directly), or Browse jobs... to see a list of recent jobs — scoped to the selected branch/tag, if one is chosen — and download from a specific row.

Package Registry tab

Has its own separate Project field, since the CI project and the one hosting the published package are often two different repositories. Enter the Package name, then either Fetch Latest Version or Browse versions... to pick a specific one.

After the download

If the downloaded file is a .zip, a picker lets you choose which file inside it is the actual firmware (a recognized extension is pre-selected automatically). Confirming loads it exactly like a local file — same Details table, same checksum, and it's added to Recent Files too. The GitLab log panel at the bottom of the dialog keeps a running history of every step, useful if a fetch fails partway through.

Tip: this feature is read-only — it only downloads artifacts/packages that already exist in GitLab. It never triggers a pipeline, uploads anything, or otherwise writes to the project.

Safety Notes When Flashing a Real ECU

  • Always try with the Virtual ECU Simulator first to make sure the firmware/ configuration is correct, before switching to real Vector hardware.
  • Run Tools → Test Connection... before the very first real flash on a new ECU.
  • Close CANoe/CANalyzer if it's open on the same channel at the same time — the app will warn you automatically if it detects a likely conflict.
  • Do not power off / disconnect the CAN wiring while a flash is in progress — this can brick the ECU.

Troubleshooting: Real Hardware Connection Errors

These messages only apply when using real Vector VN1640A/VN1630 hardware — the Virtual ECU Simulator never produces them. They show up in the Information tab (after clicking Refresh, Flash, or Tools → Test Connection...) or in a failure dialog.

python-can's Vector backend unavailable: No module named 'can'

The python-can library isn't available. Running from a built .exe: it wasn't bundled at build time — python-can must be uncommented in requirements_build.txt before running build.bat (it cannot be added to an already-built .exe). Running from source: pip install python-can.

Vector XL Driver Library error: ...

Python-can is available, but the Vector XL Driver Library itself — a separate, per-machine Windows driver, not something that travels with the .exe — isn't installed (or failed to load) on this specific machine. Install Vector Driver Setup / XL Driver Library, or open Vector Hardware Config to confirm it's already installed. If the exact same build works on another PC, this is almost always the difference between the two machines.

Connection failed: Failed to connect to Vector hardware: Channel N of application 'FlashTool' is not assigned to any interface

Vector Hardware Config hasn't been set up for this app. Open Vector Hardware Config and assign the physical channel to the application name FlashTool (see README.md, section B). Only needed on python-can versions older than 4.x that don't support selecting the channel by serial number — a newer python-can usually avoids this entirely.

Connection failed: Failed to connect to Vector hardware: ...

Any other failure while opening the CAN bus (wrong bitrate for the target ECU, hardware unplugged/ powered off, another application holding the channel exclusively, etc.) — the text after the colon is the real error from the Vector driver/python-can itself.

"A possible CAN bus conflict was detected before flashing" (Yes/No dialog, defaults to No)

Not a hard error — a pre-flight warning shown before a real (non-Virtual) flash starts, if CANoe/ CANalyzer/CANape looks like it's running, or the selected channel already looks active on the bus. Close the other tool (or stop its measurement) unless intentionally sharing the bus.
